pages.title: Bedtime Story Prompts for Kids: AI Picture Book Ideas
pages.metaDescription: Three 24-page bedtime story prompts written page by page: a hedgehog in a moonflower garden, ten sheep who won't sleep and a boy who borrows the moon.
pages.intro: A good bedtime story book slows down as it goes, until the last page is almost a whisper. These three 24-page picture books are for parents who want a bedtime story of their own and KDP sellers building a cozy list: a hedgehog who stays up for the last moonflower, a girl who settles ten restless sheep while counting to ten, and a boy afraid of the dark who borrows the moon. Each is written out page by page, with the words and the picture for every page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: End every bedtime story with the hero asleep or nearly asleep; the book should land where the child is.
Soft styles like colored pencil or paper cut-out suit bedtime better than bold comic looks.
KDP paperbacks need at least 24 pages, so each book here is 24; for home printing you can trim a few middle pages down to 16.

prompts.name: Bramble and the moonflowers

fields.title: The Night Gardener
fields.storyPrompt: A 24-page bedtime story. Every night after the village falls asleep, Mrs. Fernsby, a tall old badger in a patched blue apron, waters the moonflowers that open only in the dark. Tonight her helper Bramble, a sleepy hedgehog with a tiny lantern, wants to stay up to see the very last one bloom. He yawns through every chore: the well, the weeds, a snail moved to the lettuce. The last flower opens just for him. Bramble curls up among the glowing petals, and Mrs. Fernsby carries him home to bed. Hushed, slow and gentle.

prompts.why: Parents get a quiet, beautifully lit story that slows toward sleep, the exact mood a bedtime book has to hold.
prompts.pageStyle: Full-colour picture book illustration for a child aged 3 to 6: soft coloured-pencil look, night blues and glowing silver-white moonflowers. Mrs. Fernsby is a tall old grey badger with a striped face in a patched blue apron; Bramble is a small brown hedgehog with a tiny brass lantern. Picture at the top, a plain pale band at the bottom for text; no words in the picture; square page.

pageTexts: When the last light in the village goes out, Mrs. Fernsby puts on her patched blue apron. It is time to tend the night garden.
Bramble trots behind her with his tiny lantern. "Tonight I'm staying up," he says, and then he yawns.
The garden gate creaks open. Row after row of moonflowers wait in the dark, every bud shut tight.
"Moonflowers open only in the dark," says Mrs. Fernsby. "And the very last one waits for the deepest part of the night."
"Then I will see the very last one," says Bramble. He stands up tall to show how awake he is.
First they fill the watering can at the old stone well. Bramble holds it steady. His eyes close, just for a moment.
Splish, splash, down the long rows. Bramble lights the way, and his lantern swings slow and low.
Next come the weeds, one little tug at a time. Bramble yawns so wide that his whiskers wobble.
A snail is nibbling a moonflower leaf. Bramble carries it, very gently, to the lettuce patch instead.
Then, with a tiny sigh, the first moonflower opens. It glows like a little moon of its own.
One by one more flowers open. Soft white moths come to visit, quiet as whispers.
Bramble sits down on a flowerpot to rest. Only for a moment, he tells himself.
Mrs. Fernsby hums an old, slow tune as she ties up the tallest stems. Hum, hum, goes the night.
Hoo, hoo, says the owl in the apple tree. Even the owl sounds sleepy tonight.
Now the whole garden shines silver. All the moonflowers are open, all but one.
Bramble lies down beside the last bud to watch. He will not miss it. Not this one.
His lantern burns low. His head sinks lower. The last bud stays shut tight.
"Please," Bramble whispers, very softly. "I stayed up just for you."
And slowly, slowly, the very last moonflower opens, just for him.
It is the brightest, softest flower of all. Bramble smiles the sleepiest smile.
He curls up among the glowing petals. They are warm, and they smell like sweet milk.
Mrs. Fernsby finds him there, fast asleep. "You saw it," she whispers. "You stayed up after all."
She carries him home past the sleeping rows, the garden glowing softly behind them.
She tucks him into bed and blows out the candle. Outside, the moonflowers keep watch. Goodnight, Bramble.

prompts.name: Ten sheep who would not sleep

fields.title: Ten Sheep Who Would Not Sleep
fields.storyPrompt: A 24-page counting bedtime story. Pim, a little girl in yellow rain boots and a nightgown, can't fall asleep, so she tries counting sheep. But her ten sheep won't jump the fence: Clover wants a snack, Wooly lost her bell, the twins want one more game of tag, Hiccup has hiccups, Tuft is cold, Mumble wants a story, Little Lou wants a song, Puff's bed is lumpy and Big Bertha is scared of the dark. Pim helps each one settle, counting up to ten, until all ten snore in a woolly pile. Then Pim climbs onto the softest sheep and falls asleep too.

prompts.why: Toddlers learn to count to ten inside a bedtime routine, and short lettered pages suit parents printing at home.
prompts.pageStyle: Full-colour picture book illustration for a child aged 3 to 6: hand-drawn 2D look, simple rounded shapes, soft moonlit meadow colours. Pim is a small girl with curly black hair, a pale blue nightgown and yellow rain boots; the sheep are round, fluffy and white with black faces and legs, Big Bertha the biggest. Leave a calm empty patch of sky for the words; no words in the picture; square page.

pageTexts: Pim is not sleepy. Not one bit. The clock goes tick, tock, tick.
"I know," says Pim. "I'll count sheep!" She shuts her eyes tight.
There is the meadow. There is the fence. And there are ten sheep, all in a row.
"Jump!" says Pim. But not one sheep jumps. Not even a little hop.
"I'm hungry," says Clover. So Pim picks her a snack of sweet green clover.
Crunch, munch, yawn. Clover curls up and closes her eyes. One!
"I lost my bell," says Wooly. "I can't sleep without my bell."
Pim finds it in the daisies, ting-a-ling. Wooly snuggles down. Two!
"One more game of tag!" shout the twins, Dot and Dash. Round and round they run.
Tag, you're it, and tag, you're it! The twins flop down, puffing and giggling. Three, four!
"Hic!" says Hiccup. "Hic! I can't stop!" Each hic makes her bounce.
Pim gives her slow, slow sips of water. The hiccups float away. Five!
"Brrr," says Tuft. "The night is too chilly for me."
Pim tucks a little quilt around her, snug as a bun. Six!
"I need a story," mumbles Mumble. "Just a short one, please."
Pim tells the shortest story ever: once upon a time, a sheep fell asleep. The end. Seven!
"Sing me a song?" asks Little Lou, the smallest sheep of all.
Pim sings la-la-lullaby, soft and low. Little Lou is asleep before the end. Eight!
Puff turns round and round. "My bed is too lumpy!" Pim fluffs a pile of soft hay. Nine!
But Big Bertha is hiding behind the fence. "I'm scared of the dark," she whispers.
"Look," says Pim. "The moon is our night-light, and the stars are on too." Big Bertha looks up.
Big Bertha sighs and settles down with the others. Ten! Ten sheep, snoring in a woolly pile.
Pim yawns the biggest yawn of all. She climbs onto Big Bertha, the softest sheep.
Snore, snore, goes the meadow. And Pim? Pim is fast asleep too. Goodnight.

prompts.name: The boy who borrowed the moon

fields.title: The Boy Who Borrowed the Moon
fields.storyPrompt: A 24-page bedtime story about fear of the dark. Arlo, a boy with messy red hair who wears his blanket as a cape, is scared of the shadows in his room. One night he climbs a very tall ladder and borrows the moon as his night-light. But without the moon the owl can't hunt, the tide forgets to come in, the fireflies get lost and a fox cub can't find its way home. Arlo sees the night needs its moon more than he does. He carries it back up the ladder, and from then on the moon slips a silver beam through his window every night to keep him company.

prompts.why: Early readers who fear the dark get a story that answers the fear with wonder, a classic shape for a KDP bedtime title.
prompts.pageStyle: Full-colour picture book illustration for a child aged 6 to 9: layered paper cut-out collage look, deep night blues. Arlo is a boy with messy red hair and striped pyjamas who wears a dark blue star-patterned blanket as a cape; the moon is round and pale silver with a gentle sleepy face. Plain left side for text, picture on the right; no words in the picture; portrait 8.5 x 11 page.

pageTexts: Arlo was not afraid of spiders, or thunder, or big dogs. But he was very afraid of the dark.
At night his coat on the hook looked like a bear. His chair looked like it might creep across the floor.
One night he looked out of his window at the moon, so round and bright. And Arlo had an idea.
He tiptoed into the garden and pulled the longest ladder out of the shed.
Up he climbed, past the chimneys, past the treetops, past the sleepy clouds.
"Excuse me, Moon," said Arlo. "May I borrow you, just for tonight? I need a night-light."
The moon was surprised, but it said yes. Arlo tucked it under his arm and climbed carefully down.
He set the moon on his shelf. His whole room glowed silver, and there were no bears and no monsters at all.
But outside, the sky was black. Without the moon, the owl could not see a thing in the fields below.
Down by the harbour, the tide forgot to come in. The little boats sat stuck on the sand.
In the meadow, the fireflies got lost. They bumped into grass, and into each other, and into a very cross hedgehog.
A fox cub could not find the path home. Which way? Which way? It was much too dark to tell.
Tap, tap, tap. Arlo woke to find the owl at his window. "Where has the moon gone?" it hooted.
Arlo looked at the moon on his shelf. His cheeks went hot. "I borrowed it," he said in a small voice.
He carried the moon outside to see. There were the boats, stuck on the sand, waiting for the sea.
In the meadow, the lost fireflies blinked at him, and the fox cub was still looking for its way home.
Arlo hugged the moon tight. Then he understood. The night needed its moon more than he did.
So up the ladder he went again. The moon was heavy, and his arms were tired, but Arlo did not stop.
At the very top, he lifted the moon back into its place in the sky. "Thank you for lending me your light," he said.
At once, the tide rushed in and lifted the boats. The fireflies found their way, and the fox cub ran home.
The owl swooped happily over the fields. The night was itself again.
Arlo climbed back into bed. The corners of his room were dark again, and he felt a little bit scared.
Then a long silver moonbeam slipped through his window and lay across his blanket, soft and bright.
From then on, every night, the moon sent Arlo a moonbeam to keep him company. And Arlo was never afraid of the dark again.

pages.title: Friendship Story Prompts for Kids' Picture Books
pages.metaDescription: Three 24-page friendship picture book prompts, written page by page: a tortoise and a duckling, a lonely robot and two balcony pen pals.
pages.intro: These friendship picture books are for children aged 3 to 9 and the parents, teachers and KDP sellers who read with them: two characters who don't fit together, a problem, and the moment they realise they need each other. A slow tortoise and a speedy duckling find their way home through a flood, a lonely clock-shop robot learns a friend can't be built, and two children without a shared language trade drawings across a street. Each book is written out page by page, with the words and the picture for all 24 pages, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Make the two friends opposites (slow and fast, quiet and loud) so the story has built-in tension.
Let the friendship be tested once before the happy ending; it makes the ending earned.
Give each friend one fixed visual trait so they look the same on every page.

prompts.name: Pebble the tortoise and Dabble the duckling

fields.title: Pebble and Dabble
fields.storyPrompt: A 24-page picture book. Pebble, a careful tortoise with a moss-green shell, and Dabble, a splashy yellow duckling with one wonky feather, disagree about everything: Pebble likes slow walks and quiet, Dabble likes racing and quacking. When a storm floods the meadow, Dabble can swim but can't find the way home, and Pebble knows every path but can't swim. Pebble rides on Dabble's back and gives directions while she paddles past the fence post, the oak tree and the bridge. They get home together under a rainbow and decide being different is the best part.

prompts.why: Preschoolers see two opposite friends solve a problem together, a gentle lesson parents and teachers read again and again.

pageTexts: Pebble the tortoise lived at the edge of a sunny meadow. He liked to take things slowly.
Dabble the duckling lived by the pond. She liked to do everything fast!
One morning, Dabble zoomed around a bush and bumped right into Pebble. Bump! "Oops!" said Dabble.
"Let's be friends!" said Dabble. "Let's race to the big oak tree!"
Dabble raced. Pebble walked. By the time Pebble got there, Dabble was fast asleep.
"Let's sing loud songs!" quacked Dabble. "I like quiet," said Pebble.
Pebble liked to munch dandelions. Dabble liked to gobble pondweed.
Pebble liked to nap in the warm sun. Dabble could not sit still for one minute.
"We are too different to be friends," sighed Pebble. Dabble's wonky feather drooped.
That afternoon, big dark clouds rolled over the meadow. Whoosh went the wind.
Rain poured down. Drip, drop, splash! The meadow began to fill with water.
Dabble swam round and round. The water had covered every path. Which way was home?
On a little hill, Pebble sat on a rock. He knew every path in the meadow, but he could not swim.
"Pebble!" called Dabble. She paddled as fast as she could toward the hill.
"I can swim, but I am lost," said Dabble. "I know the way, but I can't swim," said Pebble.
Then Dabble had an idea. "Climb on my back!"
"Left at the old fence post!" said Pebble. Dabble paddled left.
"Now straight past the big oak tree!" Dabble paddled and paddled.
"Under the little bridge, then right at the bulrushes!" The rain began to stop.
At last they saw home: Pebble's cozy burrow and Dabble's nest, high and dry on the bank.
The sun came out, and a rainbow stretched over the meadow.
"You were fast when we needed fast," said Pebble. "And you were careful when we needed careful," said Dabble.
The next day, they took a slow walk and a quick swim. Then they sang a very quiet song together.
Pebble and Dabble were as different as can be. And that was the best part.

prompts.name: Cog the clock-shop robot

fields.title: Cog Builds a Friend
fields.storyPrompt: A 24-page picture book. Cog, a small rusty robot with one wobbly wheel and a lightbulb antenna, lives alone in a dusty clock-repair shop after the old clockmaker retires. He builds friends from springs and gears: a teapot dog, a pocket-watch bird, a toaster with a smile. None of them can talk back. Then Nell, a girl with a red toolbox and orange overalls, comes in looking for spare parts. She fixes Cog's wheel; he helps her finish her go-kart and fixes its steering. Cog learns a friend isn't something you build. It's someone who listens and helps.

pageTexts: At the end of a crooked street stood a little clock-repair shop, full of ticking clocks.
Inside lived Cog, a small rusty robot with one wobbly wheel. Every day he helped the old clockmaker.
Then the clockmaker grew too old to work. He hung up his apron, patted Cog's head and said goodbye.
Now the shop was quiet. Dust settled on the clocks. Cog felt very alone.
Cog's lightbulb antenna flickered. "I know," he said. "I will build a friend!"
He found an old teapot, four springs and a feather duster. Clank, twist, bolt!
He made a teapot dog that wagged its spout. But when Cog said hello, it only whistled.
Next he made a pocket-watch bird with paper-clip wings. It flapped in circles, but it could not talk back.
Then he built a toaster with a big painted smile. Cog told it a joke. Pop! went the toast.
Cog had a shop full of friends. But none of them could listen, and none of them could help.
Ding-a-ling! The shop bell rang. In walked a girl in orange overalls, carrying a red toolbox.
"Hi, I'm Nell," she said. "I'm building a go-kart. Do you have any spare wheels?"
Cog rolled forward to help. Wobble, wobble, CLUNK! His wheel fell right off.
"Don't worry," said Nell, opening her toolbox. "I can fix that."
She oiled the axle, tightened a bolt and gave the wheel a spin. Cog rolled in a perfect circle!
"Thank you!" said Cog. "Now let me help you." Cog knew where every gear and spring was hiding.
They worked in Nell's backyard all afternoon. Nell hammered. Cog held the boards steady.
But when Nell tried it, the go-kart would not steer. It rolled straight into the hedge. Crunch!
Cog thought hard. His lightbulb glowed. "It needs a clock spring for the steering!"
Nell climbed in. Cog hopped on the back. Down the hill they went, steering left and right!
At the bottom, they laughed until they fell over. "We make a good team," said Nell.
That evening, Nell asked, "Can I come back tomorrow?" Cog's antenna glowed its brightest ever.
Cog looked at his teapot dog, his watch bird and his smiling toaster. They were fun. But Nell was different.
A friend isn't something you build. A friend is someone who listens and helps. And now Cog had one.

fields.storyPrompt: A 24-page picture book. pageTexts: Mateo lived on the fourth floor. From his balcony he could see the whole narrow street.
One windy morning, a moving van stopped across the street.
Soon a girl with a red hair clip stepped onto the balcony opposite. Mateo waved. She waved back.
"Hello!" called Mateo. The girl called something back, but Mateo didn't know her words.
She didn't know his words either. They both shrugged, and then they both laughed.
That night, Mateo had an idea. He found a long rope, a basket and two pulley wheels in Grandpa's toolbox.
Grandpa helped him send the rope across. Hana caught it and tied it to her railing.
Mateo drew a picture of himself with a big smile. He put it in the basket and pulled. Squeak, squeak, squeak.
Hana unfolded the drawing and smiled. Then she drew one back, with her name underneath: Hana.
After that, the basket went back and forth every day after school.
Mateo sent a picture of Pepe. Hana sent a picture of her goldfish, Bubbles.
Hana sent almond cookies wrapped in paper. Mateo sent oranges from his mother's market bag.
They folded paper boats and sent a whole fleet across the street.
Mateo drew a sun and wrote his word for it. Hana wrote her word underneath. Now they had two words for sun.
Every day they learned new words: rain, cat, bread, friend.
One morning, the basket did not come back. Hana's balcony was empty.
Mateo waited all day. What if she had moved away?
The next day, the basket squeaked over. Inside was a drawing of Hana in bed with a thermometer. She had a cold!
Mateo sent a get-well drawing, his warm striped scarf and a little jar of honey from Mom.
A few days later, Hana came back out, smiling and wearing his scarf.
Then Hana sent a new drawing: the bakery downstairs, and a clock pointing to four.
At four o'clock, they both walked into the bakery. They stood by the bread and felt very, very shy.
Then Hana took a pencil from her pocket, and Mateo grabbed a paper napkin.
Together they drew two balconies, one rope, and two friends in the middle. They didn't need any words at all.

pages.title: Bravery Story Book Prompts: Picture Books About Overcoming Fears
pages.metaDescription: Bravery picture book prompts, 24 pages each and written page by page: a monster scared of the dark, the deep end of the pool and night noises.
pages.intro: Children's fears are real to them, and a picture book about bravery shows that being brave means feeling scared and trying anyway. These three stories tackle classic fears with warmth and a little humour: a boy and the monster under his bed, a girl who won't go past the rope into the deep end, and a girl tracking down the noises of an old house at night. Each book is written out page by page, with the words and the picture for all 24 pages, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool. Parents use them to talk through a specific worry, and KDP sellers find steady demand in the emotional-growth niche.
tips: Name the exact fear in the brief (the dark, swimming, a noise at night) so the story meets the child where they are.
Let the scary thing turn out smaller, sillier or kinder than expected.
Show bravery as small steps across several pages, not one sudden leap.

pageTexts: This is Milo. Every night he puts on his fuzzy dinosaur slippers and gets ready for bed.
Mum reads him a story, tucks him in and turns off the big light.
Scritch, scratch. Something is under the bed!
Milo pulls the blanket over his head. It must be a monster.
A big spiky shadow stretches across the wall. It has long, long arms!
Milo reaches for his flashlight. His hand is shaking.
He counts to three. One... two... three!
Milo leans over the edge and peeks under the bed.
Two big eyes blink back at him. It IS a monster!
But the monster is small. And he is shaking even more than Milo.
"I'm Gus," whispers the monster. "I'm scared of the dark up there on top of your bed."
A monster who is scared of the dark? Milo thinks hard. Maybe he is not the only one.
"Come out, Gus," says Milo. "I want to show you something."
Milo switches on his moon night-light. A soft glow fills the room.
Then Milo gives Gus his teddy. Teddy is very good at hugs.
Gus points at the wall. The spiky shadow is back!
Gus waddles over and lifts the shadow's long arm. It is only Milo's raincoat!
And the spiky head? It's just Milo's kite, hanging on its hook.
Milo laughs. Gus laughs. The shadows are not scary at all.
They make shadow animals with the flashlight: a bunny, a bird and a wobbly dinosaur.
It is very late now. Where will Gus sleep?
"Let's be brave together," says Milo. Gus climbs up onto the big bed.
They snuggle under the blanket, with the night-light glowing and the flashlight on.
Under the bed it is quiet now. And on top, two brave friends are fast asleep.

pageTexts: On the first day of summer, Nora runs to the town pool with her goggles pushed up on her forehead.
The pool is full of splashing. Her friends race straight to the deep end.
Nora stops at the rope. Past it, the water turns dark blue and very, very deep.
"Jump in, Nora!" calls her friend Theo from the diving board.
Nora shakes her head. She sits on the edge and dangles her toes in instead.
Every day it is the same. Nora watches. Nora waits. Nora stays dry.
One afternoon, Grandma arrives in her flowered swim cap. Long ago, she was a lifeguard right here.
Grandma sits down beside Nora. "Being brave doesn't mean you're not scared," she says. "It means trying one small thing."
Week one is bubbles. Nora puts her face in the water and hums. Bubbles tickle her nose.
At first Nora pops straight back up, coughing and blinking. Grandma just smiles. "Again."
By Friday, Nora can blow bubbles for a slow count of ten.
Week two is floating. "Be a starfish," says Grandma.
Grandma lets go a little. Then a little more. Nora floats all by herself!
Week three is kicking. Nora holds a foam board and kicks across the shallow end.
Kick, kick, kick to Grandma. Each time, Grandma stands a little farther away.
Week four, Nora swims all the way to the rope and touches it. She doesn't cross it. Not yet.
That night, Nora dreams of the deep end. In her dream, the water is warm and full of friendly fish.
Week five, Grandma floats out in the deep end. "I'm right here," she says.
Nora ducks under the rope. Her feet can't touch the bottom. She makes a starfish, and she floats.
On the last day of summer, the pool is crowded and the sun is low and golden.
Nora walks to the edge of the deep end. Her toes curl over the side.
She takes a big breath. One small thing, she thinks. Then she jumps.
Splash! Nora bobs up laughing, and Grandma is right there.
As they walk home, Nora's hair is still dripping. "Next summer," she says, "I'm trying the diving board."

pageTexts: Ivy and her family have moved to an old house at the edge of the woods.
Her new room is up in the roof, with a sloping ceiling and a round window.
At bedtime, Dad says goodnight and the whole house goes dark.
Then the old house begins to make noises.
CLANK. CLANK. Something is banging in the corner of her room.
Ivy wraps her yellow scarf around her neck, grabs her torch and climbs out of bed.
She tiptoes to the corner. The clanking is only the old radiator, warming up for the night.
One noise found. Ivy feels a tiny bit braver.
Whooo. Whooo. A whisper is coming from somewhere downstairs.
Ivy follows the whisper down the creaky stairs. Every single step goes eek.
The whisper is loudest in the living room, by the big stone fireplace.
She shines her torch up the chimney. It's only the wind, blowing over the roof.
Tap. Tap. Tap. Something is knocking at the window!
Ivy's heart thumps. She counts to three and pulls back the curtain.
It's just a branch of the old oak tree, tapping in the breeze.
A round brown owl on the branch blinks at her. Ivy waves, and the owl hoots back.
Drip. Drip. Drip. Ivy follows a new sound into the kitchen.
She stands on a stool and turns the old tap tight. The dripping stops. Ivy is getting good at this.
THUMP! THUMP-THUMP! Something big is upstairs, right above her head.
This noise is the scariest of all. Ivy takes a deep breath and climbs the stairs again.
She pushes open her bedroom door and shines her torch inside...
It's Pickle! He is leaping after a fluttering moth.
Ivy laughs so hard she has to sit down. Pickle looks very pleased with himself.
Ivy climbs back into bed with Pickle. Clank, whoosh, tap, drip. The old house hums like a friend, and Ivy falls asleep.

pageTexts: This is Momo. Momo is a little panda, and Momo is getting big.
One morning, Mama Panda has a surprise. A big box with a red bow!
Inside is a shiny green potty. It is just for Momo.
Momo sits on his potty with his shorts on. Hello, potty!
Teddy wants a turn too. Teddy sits on the potty. Good sitting, Teddy!
Mama reads Momo a potty book. Wee and poo go in the potty, she says.
Momo sits on the potty. He waits. And waits. Nothing happens.
That's okay, says Mama. We try again later.
Momo plays with his blocks. He builds a tall, tall tower.
Momo is so busy. He forgets to listen to his tummy.
Oops! An accident. Momo's shorts are wet. Momo feels sad.

After lunch, Momo drinks his water. Glug, glug, glug.
Momo listens to his tummy. His tummy says, potty time!
Run, Momo, run! Down the hall to the bathroom.
Shorts down. Sit down. Momo sits on his green potty.
Momo waits. He sings a little song. And then... it works!
Momo did it! Momo used the potty! Mama claps and claps.

Wash, wash, wash your paws. Lots and lots of bubbles.
Momo puts a shiny star on his sticker chart. One star for Momo!
Momo gets brand-new big-kid pants, with green bamboo leaves all over.
Momo listens to his tummy now. Momo is a big-kid panda!

pageTexts: STOMP, STOMP, ROAR! This is Rory. Rory is a little dinosaur with a very big roar.
Rory has a brand-new potty. It is orange, just like his spots.
Potty time, Rory? asks Mum. No time! says Rory. I'm too busy stomping!
Rory stomps through the kitchen. STOMP! The spoons rattle. CLATTER, CLATTER!
Rory roars at Pickle the cat. ROAR! Pickle jumps up on the fridge. MEOW!
Rory builds a tower. Block, block, block. Higher and higher!
Rory's tail wiggles. His feet wiggle. But Rory keeps on building.
CRASH! Down comes the tower. Uh-oh. Rory's shorts are wet. Rory's roar is very small.
Dad gives Rory a big dino hug. That's okay, little dino. Next time, stomp to the potty!
Clean shorts, dry socks. Rory is ready to stomp again.
Rory stomps in the garden. SPLASH! Right in a muddy puddle.

HOORAY! cheers Mum. HOORAY! cheers Dad. They cheer so loud the walls shake.

pageTexts: In a castle on a hill lived a little princess called Plum. Her crown was always a little bit crooked.
One morning the Queen had a royal surprise. A present with a big purple bow!
Inside was a tiny golden throne with a soft velvet cushion. A potty, just for Plum!
Every princess needs her own throne, said the Queen. This one is yours.
Plum patted her little throne. Hello, throne. But I'm very busy today!
Plum fed the castle ducks by the moat. Quack, quack, quack!
Plum had tea with Bramble the dragon. More tea, Bramble? Bramble puffed a tiny smoke ring.
Plum danced in the ballroom. Twirl, twirl, twirl went her dress.
Then Plum felt a funny feeling in her tummy. But she kept on twirling.
Oh no! A royal accident, right in the middle of the ballroom.
Plum's lip wobbled. Princesses don't have accidents, she sniffed.
The Queen knelt down and whispered a secret. Even queens had accidents once.
When I was little, I had one on the castle stairs! said the Queen. Plum giggled.
Plum put on a clean dress and her favourite pink shoes. All better.
Accidents happen, said the Queen. We just try again.
The next day, Plum listened to her tummy. Tummy, do you need the throne?
Yes! Plum hurried down the long hall, past the knights and the paintings.
Plum sat on her golden throne. She waited like a princess, very still and very patient.
Bramble waited outside the door. The ducks waited too.
And then... she did it! Plum made it to her throne in time!
Ta-ra-ra! The trumpets played. The whole court cheered. The ducks quacked!
Plum washed her hands in the royal basin, with lots and lots of bubbles.
The Queen gave Plum a little golden box. Inside were big-girl crown pants!
Plum stood tall. I'm a big-girl princess now! And this time, her crown stayed perfectly straight.

pages.intro: A first day of school story book helps a child picture the day before it happens, and shows that other kids, and even teachers, feel nervous too. pageTexts: Today is Kit's very first day at Hollow Oak School.
Kit's tummy feels wobbly. She can only eat half her toast.
Dad packs her lunch: crackers, apple slices, and something else Kit doesn't see.
Her new blue backpack is so big it nearly tips her over.
Kit holds Dad's paw all the way down the forest path.
There it is: Hollow Oak School, inside the biggest tree in the whole wood.
Kit holds on until the very last second. "I'll be back at pickup," says Dad.
Dad waves. Kit waves back. Then he is gone.
The classroom is loud. Bunnies hop, squirrels chatter, and Kit doesn't know anyone.
Mrs. Burrow shows Kit her very own hook, with a little fox sticker above it.
Everyone sings the morning song. Kit doesn't know the words, so she just listens.
At the painting table, Kit paints her den. It makes her miss home even more.
In the corner sits a tiny owlet. She looks wobbly too.
At playtime, Kit stands by the fence and thinks about Dad.
Then the lunch bell rings. Everyone sits at the long log table.
Kit opens her lunchbox. On top of the crackers is a folded note.
Inside is a drawing of two foxes holding paws. Kit knows exactly who drew it.
Kit feels warm all over, like a hug from Dad.
Wren has forgotten her snack. Kit holds out her crackers. "Want to share?"
Wren takes one and smiles. Crunch, crunch. Soon they are both giggling.
In the afternoon, Kit draws a picture of her own, just for Dad.
At story time, Kit and Wren sit side by side on the rug.
At pickup, there is Dad, right where he said he'd be!
Kit gives Dad her drawing: two foxes and one new friend. "Can I come back tomorrow?" she asks.

Gemma has to duck way, way down to get inside.

pageTexts: Jayden woke up before his alarm. Today he was starting first grade, and his tummy already felt fizzy.
Across town, Ms. Okafor was awake early too. It was her first day teaching at Maple Street School.
Jayden stared at his cereal. "I'm not hungry," he told Mom.
Ms. Okafor stared at her toast. She wasn't hungry either.
Jayden checked his rocket backpack. Pencils, lunch, water bottle. Then he checked it again. And again.
Ms. Okafor checked her bag three times: markers, stickers and her shiny new name badge.
On the walk to school, Jayden's tummy was full of butterflies.
A few streets away, so was Ms. Okafor's.
Maple Street School looked enormous. There were so many kids, and Jayden didn't know a single one.

She hurried down the hallway with a box of books. She didn't notice something slip from her bag.

Jayden held out the badge. "Is this yours?"
Ms. Okafor knelt down. "Thank you," she whispered. "Can I tell you a secret? It's my first day here too."
"Mine too," said Jayden. "I couldn't eat my breakfast." "Neither could I!" laughed Ms. Okafor.

pageTexts: Bao was the loudest one in his family. He sang loud, he laughed loud, and he played his drum loudest of all.
Boom, boom, boom! went Bao's drum every morning. Mama covered her ears, but she was smiling.
One day Mama's tummy was big and round. "Soon you will be a big brother," said Baba.
Bao helped get the baby's room ready. He put his old teddy bear in the crib, so the baby would have a friend.
Then baby Lin came home. She was tiny and pink and very, very quiet.
Everyone tiptoed. Everyone whispered. Lin stayed quiet for one whole minute.
"WAAAAH!" Lin was even louder than Bao!
Lin cried at breakfast. Bao's cereal went soggy while Mama rocked her.
Lin cried at bath time. Even the squeaky duck did not help.
Lin cried in the middle of the night. Bao pulled his pillow over his head.
Mama and Baba yawned all day long. "Not now, Bao," they said. "Maybe later."

Mama peeked in. "Bao," she whispered, "how did you do that?"
"I'm the baby drummer," Bao whispered back. Mama gave him the biggest, quietest hug.
Now every night Bao plays his soft, slow song. Lin falls asleep, and Mama and Baba finally get some rest.
On Saturday, Baba took Bao to the park, just the two of them. They drummed on a bucket and on the big metal slide.
In the mornings the whole family plays loud music, and Lin kicks and giggles. But at night, Bao is the gentlest drummer in the world.

pageTexts: Olive was a small hedgehog with a pink acorn hat. Her favorite place in the whole wide world was Mama's lap.
On Mama's lap, Olive heard stories, ate warm blackberry toast, and fell asleep to Mama's humming.
One spring, Mama's tummy began to grow. "A baby is coming," Mama said.
Mama's tummy grew bigger. Olive's spot on the lap grew smaller.
By summer there was hardly any lap at all. Olive perched on the very edge and held on tight.
Then one morning the baby came. His name was Bramble, and he was very, very small.
Now Mama's lap was full of baby. Bramble ate on the lap. Bramble slept on the lap.
"Is there room for me?" asked Olive. "In a little while, love," said Mama.
So Olive put on her hat and went looking for a new lap.
She tried Papa's lap. It was bouncy and knobbly, and Papa could not keep his knees still.
She tried Grandpa's lap. It was cozy, but Grandpa snored, and his snore blew her hat right off.
She tried Biscuit the cat's back. Biscuit did not think that was a good idea at all.
She tried a pile of cushions, a basket of wool and a mossy log. None of them were quite right.
Olive sat on the doorstep and sniffed. "Nobody has a lap for me anymore."
That evening, Mama found her there. "There you are," said Mama softly. "I've been looking for you."
Mama carried Olive inside to the big armchair by the fire.
She put baby Bramble on one side. Then she patted the other side. "And this side is for Olive."
Olive snuggled in. It was a little squished, but it was warm, and it smelled like Mama.
Mama opened a storybook. "This one is for both of you," she said.
Bramble wrapped his tiny paw around Olive's finger. Olive held very, very still.
"He likes you," whispered Mama. "You're his big sister."
On Sunday, Papa minded Bramble, and Mama took Olive blackberry picking, just the two of them.
Now every evening there are three in the big armchair. Olive turns the pages while Mama reads.
Olive learned that a lap can stretch, and there will always be room for her.

pageTexts: Marcus was seven, and he knew a lot about a lot. So when Mom said a baby brother was coming, he grabbed a notebook. "Somebody has to write the rules," he said.
On the very first page he wrote: The Official Big Brother Handbook. By Marcus. Do not touch.
Rule one: Babies are boring. They don't play soccer, they don't tell jokes, and they can't even sit up.
Rule two: Never share your room. Marcus taped a sign to his door, just in case.
Rule three: Big brothers do not change diapers. Ever. Marcus underlined that one three times.
Rule four: Big brothers do not sing lullabies. Lullabies are for babies, and Marcus was definitely not a baby.
Mom's belly got bigger. Dad built a crib and had six screws left over. Marcus kept writing.
Then one night Grandma came to stay, and Mom and Dad hurried off to the hospital.
Two days later they came home with Miles. He was tiny, wrinkly and fast asleep.
"Want to hold him?" asked Dad. Marcus sat very still on the couch while Dad put Miles in his arms.
Miles opened his eyes. Then he grabbed Marcus's finger and squeezed. Marcus took out his pencil and crossed out Rule one.
Miles was not boring at all. He sneezed like a kitten, frowned like a grumpy old man and hiccuped for ten whole minutes.
But Miles also cried. A lot. Mom and Dad were always busy with bottles, burps and diapers.
Nobody asked about Marcus's soccer game. He wrote a new rule: Rule five: Babies hog all the grown-ups.
That Saturday, Grandma looked after Miles, and Dad took Marcus to the park, just the two of them. They kicked the ball until the sun went down.
"You're still my number one striker," said Dad. Marcus grinned and crossed out Rule five.
One night Miles cried and cried. Mom was so tired she was nearly asleep standing up.
Marcus didn't know any lullabies. So he sang the only song he knew by heart: his soccer team's cheer.
Miles stopped crying. He stared at Marcus. Then he laughed his very first laugh. Rule four: crossed out.
When Miles grew too big for his bassinet, Mom asked if his crib could go in Marcus's room. Marcus thought about it for a long, long time.
Then he took the sign off his door. Rule two: crossed out.
Rule three he kept. Mostly. Holding the wipes is not the same as changing a diaper.
One rainy afternoon Miles fell asleep on Marcus's chest. Marcus didn't move for a whole hour.
On the last page of the handbook, every old rule was crossed out. Only one rule was left, in big letters: Be the best big brother ever.

pageTexts: High on a snowy hill, in a cosy cave, lived a little teal dragon named Saffron.
Saffron had stubby wings, big amber eyes and a tail that curled like a snail shell.
But Saffron had a secret. She was afraid of fire.
Whenever she sneezed, sparks flew out of her nose. Ah... ah... ACHOO!
The sparks scared her so much that she hid under her blanket all day long.
One morning, a boy named Toby came up the hill with a basket.
"Hello! I heard a sneeze," said Toby. "Are you all right?"
"I'm scared of my own fire," whispered Saffron. "It's too hot and too big."
Toby smiled. "Let's start teeny-tiny. Can you toast just one marshmallow?"
Saffron took a deep breath and puffed. Out came a flame as small as a candle.
The marshmallow turned golden brown. "I did it!" cheered Saffron.
The next day, Toby took Saffron to the village bakery. The big oven had gone cold.
Saffron blew a soft, steady flame, and soon the oven glowed warm and orange.
Out came warm loaves and sticky buns. The whole bakery smelled sweet.
Then they went to the pond, where the ice was too thick for the ducks to swim.
Saffron breathed a warm, gentle flame, and the ice melted into a round pool.
"Quack, quack!" said the ducks. Saffron felt a little bit brave.
That night was the Winter Lantern Festival. Everyone hung paper lanterns in the square.
Then a big, cold wind went WHOOSH! Every single lantern blew out.
The square was dark, and the children were scared. "Who can help?" they asked.
Saffron's knees shook. Then she remembered the marshmallow, the oven and the pond.
She flew from lantern to lantern, puffing a tiny flame into each one.
Soon the whole square glowed gold. "Hooray for Saffron!" everyone cheered.
Now Saffron lights the lanterns every winter, and she isn't afraid anymore.

pageTexts: In the kingdom of Crumblewick, there lived a young knight named Sir Wobbles.
His armor was three sizes too big, so he clanked, clonked and wobbled wherever he went.
One morning, a terrible ROAR rolled down from the mountain. Every window in the castle rattled.
The King called his knights. "Who will stop the dragon?" Everyone stepped back, except Sir Wobbles, who tripped forward.
"Sir Wobbles it is!" said the King. Sir Wobbles gulped.
He set off on his pony, Pudding, with his sword, his shield and a bag of jam sandwiches.
The mountain path was steep and twisty. Clank. Clonk. Oops!
The roars grew louder. The trees shook. Sir Wobbles' knees knocked together.
At the top, he tripped over his own sword and flew through the air...
...and landed right on the dragon's nose. BONK!
The dragon was huge and red, with a yellow belly. But he didn't look fierce. He looked miserable.
"Ow, ow, owwww," moaned the dragon. "I'm Grumbold, and I have a terrible toothache."
"I ate all of the baker's toffee," sniffed Grumbold. "Now my tooth wobbles even more than you do."
Sir Wobbles had an idea. "Wait right here. I know just who can help!"
He fetched Dr. Molar, the castle dentist, with her giant pliers and her tiny round glasses.
When the kingdom heard the roar was only a toothache, everyone came along with ropes and ladders.
Dr. Molar climbed a ladder and peered into Grumbold's mouth. "There's the wobbly one!"
But the pliers were far too small for a dragon tooth. "We need a rope!" said Dr. Molar.
Sir Wobbles tied the rope around the tooth with a big, wobbly knot.
The whole kingdom grabbed the rope: the King, the baker, the children and even Pudding the pony.
"One, two, three... PULL!" They pulled and pulled and PULLED.
POP! Out came the tooth, and everyone tumbled into a giant heap.
Grumbold smiled a gappy smile. "Thank you! I feel wonderful!"
From then on, Grumbold was the kingdom's best friend. He gave rides on Sundays and never ate toffee again.

pageTexts: In a mountain village where winter lasted half the year, there lived a girl named Saskia.
One evening, while she was gathering firewood, she saw something glowing in the snow.
It was an egg, silver and speckled, and as warm as fresh bread.
She carried it home, wrapped it in wool and set it beside the fire.
At midnight, the egg cracked. Out tumbled a tiny silver dragon.
He sneezed a puff of warm smoke. "I'll call you Cinder," she whispered.
Cinder loved warm goat's milk, roasted chestnuts and sleeping inside Saskia's hood.
Saskia hid him in the old barn behind the hay bales, where no one ever looked.
Every day, Cinder grew bigger. Soon he was the size of a goat, and then the size of a pony.
On the icy lake, Saskia taught him to fly. He flapped, he slid, and he flopped.
Then one bright morning, Cinder lifted into the sky, and Saskia cheered until her voice was hoarse.
At night, they flew together above the sleeping village, under a sky full of stars.
But Cinder kept on growing. One morning, his head poked straight through the barn roof.
The villagers saw him. "A dragon!" they cried, and they slammed their doors and shutters.
Cinder hid his face under his wings. He did not understand why they were afraid of him.
That night, Cinder stared at the clouds, where shapes like dragons drifted across the moon.
Saskia's heart ached, but she knew. "You belong up there, with the other dragons."
At dawn, she climbed onto his back, and they flew toward the highest peak.
Above the clouds was a land of ice and gold, where great dragons slept on the mountaintops.
An old golden dragon bowed her head to Saskia. "Thank you for keeping him warm."
Saskia hugged Cinder one last time. "Don't forget me," she said.
Cinder carried her home and left a single silver scale in her hand.
The winter was long, and Saskia missed him every single day.
But every spring, a silver dragon circles the village, and wherever his shadow falls, the snow melts early.

She stuffed her cheeks. She filled her paws. She even balanced acorns on her head.
"Could you spare a few?" asked Pip and Posy, the little field mice. "No," said Nutmeg. "They are all mine."
The jays asked too. Nutmeg hid her pile behind her tail. "Mine, mine, mine!"
Then Nutmeg began to hide her acorns. She dug a hole under the big oak.
She tucked some under a stone by the stream.
She buried some in the meadow by the fence.
She dug and hid until the whole wood was full of little bumps. "Now I have plenty," she yawned.
Down in their burrow, Pip and Posy stored a few seeds each day and shared them with each other.
Then the snow came, soft and white, and covered everything.
One cold morning, Nutmeg woke up hungry. "Time for an acorn," she said.
But the wood was all white. Where was the oak hole? Where was the stream stone? Nutmeg could not remember.
She dug and dug. She found a pinecone. Not an acorn.
She dug again. She found a pebble. Not an acorn either.
Nutmeg sat on a branch. Her tummy rumbled. She had hidden so much, and now she had nothing.
Pip and Posy saw her from their burrow. "Poor Nutmeg," said Posy.
"Come in, come in!" called Pip. "It's warm inside."
The mice shared their seeds and berries. "I'm sorry I didn't share," said Nutmeg. "Thank you for sharing with me."
At last spring came. In the corner of her nest, Nutmeg found a few acorns she had kept.
This time she didn't hide them. She gave one to Pip, one to Posy and one to each jay.
"Let's plant them," said Nutmeg. So they all planted acorns across the wood.
Rain fell and the sun shone. Little oak trees popped up everywhere, even where Nutmeg's lost acorns lay.
Now Hazel Wood has acorns enough for everyone. What you give away comes back to you, and grows.

pageTexts: Rufus was a young fox who lived beside Redrock Canyon. He thought he was the fastest, cleverest fox in the world.
"Too slow!" he laughed as he raced past the rabbits. The rabbits did not laugh.
One morning, Rufus climbed all the way to the top of the canyon.
"I'm the fastest fox in the world!" he shouted. "...fastest fox in the world!" the canyon shouted back.
Rufus grinned. Someone over there was listening. So he shouted, "You're slow and silly!"
"You're slow and silly!" came the answer. Rufus's ears went flat. Who would dare say that to him?
He peered across the canyon. "There must be another fox hiding over there," he growled.
"Your tail is scruffy!" he yelled. "Your tail is scruffy!" the voice yelled back. "Go away!" "Go away!"
Rufus climbed down into the canyon to find the rude fox. He found only a lizard, sunning on a stone.
All afternoon he shouted rude things, and all afternoon the rude things came right back.
By sunset his voice was a croak. He felt tired and sad. The rabbits had gone home without him.
Then soft wings swept down beside him. It was Sorrel, the old grey owl.
"Another fox is being horrible to me," Rufus croaked. "He copies every word."
Sorrel blinked slowly. "No one is there, Rufus. The canyon gives back what you give it. Tomorrow, try kind words."
That night Rufus lay awake in his den, thinking about everything he had shouted.
At dawn he went back to the edge. He took a deep breath.
"You're a good friend!" he called. "...a good friend!" sang the canyon. Rufus's tail began to wag.
"Have a wonderful day!" "...wonderful day!" Rufus laughed, and the canyon laughed with him.
Then Rufus thought about the rabbits. His words to them had come back too, as frowns and empty meadows.
He found them in the clover. "I'm sorry I called you slow," he said. "You're the best hoppers I know."
The rabbits smiled. "Want to play hide-and-seek?" they asked. And for the first time, they played together.
Rufus told the badgers their tunnel was amazing. They showed him every room and shared their blackberries.
That evening, all his new friends stood on the canyon edge and shouted kind words, and the canyon sent every one back.
Rufus had learned what the canyon knew all along. The words you send out are the words that come back.

pageTexts: On the Willow River lived Barley, a proud young beaver with a notch in his front tooth.
"I will build the biggest dam on the whole river," Barley told everyone. "All by myself!"
Chomp, chomp, chomp! Barley gnawed down his first tree.
He dragged the log to the river. It was heavy, but he did not stop.
"We can roll stones for the bottom," said the otters. "No thanks," said Barley. "I can do it alone."
"We can bring mud for the cracks," said the muskrats. "I don't need help," said Barley.
"We can weave reeds along the top," quacked the ducks. Barley just walked past.
Barley worked all day and all night, by himself.
His dam went up fast. It was tall! But it was thin, and water trickled through the gaps.
His neighbours watched from the bank. "That dam won't hold," whispered a muskrat.
Then one evening, dark clouds rolled over the valley. A spring storm was coming.
The rain poured. The river rose higher and higher and pushed against Barley's dam.
CRACK! The dam burst apart, and every stick went tumbling away down the river.
In the morning, Barley sat by a few broken sticks. He felt very small and very ashamed.
Then he heard footsteps. The otters, the muskrats and the ducks were coming, even though he had sent them away.
"I'm sorry," said Barley. "I was wrong to say no. Will you help me build a dam?" "Of course," said the otters.
The otters rolled big stones into a strong, wide base.
Barley laid thick logs on top, fitting them tight together.
The muskrats packed mud into every crack, and Barley patted it smooth with his tail.
The ducks wove reeds along the top, in and out, in and out.
When it was finished, the new dam was wide and strong. Everyone had helped build it.
That night another storm came. The friends huddled in Barley's lodge and listened to the rain.
In the morning, the dam was still standing. Behind it lay a calm pond for everyone to share.
So they had a party on the dam they had built together. Barley had learned that many paws make strong work.

pageTexts: On the morning of [Name]'s birthday, something crinkles under the pillow. It is a rolled-up map tied with red string.
The map shows [Name]'s own house, but it looks like a treasure island. A dotted path leads to a big gold X.
A clue is tucked into the corner: "Start where the green things grow." [Name] grabs a compass. Biscuit wants to come too.
[Name] opens the back door and gasps. The backyard has turned into a jungle!
The garden hose has become a rushing river. [Name] grabs a vine and swings across. Biscuit jumps the stones.
"Up here!" squawks the parrot. Inside a coconut, [Name] finds a shiny red key and the next clue.
The clue leads inside, but the living room floor is hot lava! [Name] hops from cushion to cushion. Don't touch the floor!
Under the coffee table is a blue key and a clue that says: "Set sail where the bubbles live."
[Name] pushes open the bathroom door. The bathtub is a pirate ship, ready to sail!
Here comes [Name]'s family in pirate hats. "Captain [Name], your crew is ready!" they shout.
A bubble storm rolls in! Waves of foam splash over the side. [Name] holds the wheel and steers them through.
When the storm calms down, a friendly octopus pops up. "Happy birthday!" she says, and hands over a green key.
The next clue says, "Climb high and look for smoke." From the treehouse, [Name] spots puffs of smoke coming from the garden shed.
[Name]'s friends arrive at the gate with flashlights. "We heard there's treasure!" they say. "Can we help?"
The old garden shed is now a dragon's cave. Two big eyes blink in the dark. Everyone holds hands.
Out steps a big green dragon. On the end of his tail hangs a gold key. "I am Moss," he rumbles. "I guard the last key."
But Moss looks sad. "Nobody ever asks a dragon to a birthday party," he sighs.
"Then come to mine!" says [Name]. Moss smiles so big that he puffs out smoke rings, and he gives [Name] the gold key.
"Hold on tight!" says Moss. He flies everyone over the garden, and there under the old oak tree is the big gold X.
Everyone digs and digs. Biscuit digs fastest of all. Then a spade hits something hard. Clunk!
It is a treasure chest with four keyholes: red, blue, green and gold. [Name] has every key.
Click, click, click, click. The lid creaks open, and golden light spills out.
Inside is a birthday crown and a note: "Happy Birthday, [Name]! You are [age]!" Everyone cheers.
That evening, Moss lights the [age] candles with one tiny puff of flame. It is the best birthday treasure hunt ever.

pages.title: Kindness and Sharing Story Book Prompts for Kids
pages.metaDescription: Three 24-page kindness picture book prompts, written page by page: a mouse shares her last strawberry, a lonely neighbor's bench, a giant's apples.
pages.intro: These kindness and sharing picture books are for children aged 3 to 9 and the parents, preschool teachers and KDP sellers who read with them. A field mouse shares the last strawberry of summer, a girl and her friends cheer up a lonely neighbor on his bench, and a gentle giant gives her spare apples to a hungry village. Each book is written out page by page, with the words and the picture for all 24 pages, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Make sharing cost the hero something; giving away the last strawberry means more than giving extras.
Show kindness coming back in a way the child can see on the last page.
Teachers buy these for SEL units, so keep the moral clear but let the story carry it.

fields.storyPrompt: A 24-page picture book. Mabel, a tiny field mouse with a straw basket and a daisy behind one ear, finds the very last strawberry of summer and plans to eat it all by herself. On the way home she meets a hungry hedgehog, a tired snail and a sad little sparrow. Mabel cuts the strawberry into four pieces, one for each of them. The next morning her new friends arrive with blueberries, sunflower seeds and a walnut, and together they have the biggest picnic in the meadow.

pageTexts: Mabel was a tiny field mouse who loved strawberries more than anything in the world.
But summer was almost over, and the strawberry patch was nearly empty.
Then Mabel saw it. One last strawberry, hiding under a leaf!
She pulled and she tugged. Pop! The strawberry was hers.
"I will eat it all by myself," said Mabel. "Every single bite."
Mabel set off for home, humming a happy little song.
By the bramble bush sat a hedgehog. His tummy went grumble, grumble, grumble.
"I haven't eaten all day," said Bramble. Mabel held her basket a little tighter.
Mabel said goodbye and walked on. But she couldn't stop thinking about Bramble.
On a flat stone sat a snail. She looked very, very tired.
"I have crawled all morning to find something sweet," sighed Shelly. "And I found nothing at all."
Under the old fence, a little sparrow was crying. "The big birds ate all the berries," sniffed Pip.
Mabel looked at her strawberry. Then she looked back at the hedgehog, the snail and the sparrow.
It was her very last strawberry. Mabel thought and thought and thought.
"Come here, everyone!" Mabel called.
Snip, snip, snip! Mabel cut the strawberry into four pieces.
One for Bramble, one for Shelly, one for Pip, and one for Mabel.
It was the sweetest strawberry ever, because they ate it together.
Mabel's basket was empty, but her heart felt full.
That night, Mabel slept in her cosy burrow and dreamed about her new friends.
Knock, knock! In the morning, Bramble came with blueberries stuck on his spikes.
Shelly brought sunflower seeds, and Pip brought a big round walnut.
They spread out a picnic. It was the biggest picnic in the whole meadow!
Sharing one little strawberry had brought Mabel a whole meadow of friends.

pageTexts: Every day after school, Zuri rode her purple scooter down Maple Street. Whoosh!
And every day she passed Mr. Ike, sitting all by himself on the bench outside his building.
He wore a flat cap and fed crumbs to one pigeon. Nobody ever stopped to say hello.
"Why is Mr. Ike always by himself?" Zuri asked at dinner. "Maybe he's lonely," said Mom.
That night, Zuri drew a picture of the bench, the big tree and a bright yellow sun.
The next afternoon, Zuri and Mom stopped at the bench. Zuri's tummy felt fluttery.
"This is for you," said Zuri. Mr. Ike held the drawing as if it were treasure.
"Did you know I planted this tree?" he said. "It was no taller than you, a long, long time ago."
He told her how he planted it with his papa, the summer they moved to Maple Street.
When they left, Mr. Ike waved the drawing in the air. "Come back soon!" he called.
At school, Zuri told her friends Leo and Amira all about Mr. Ike and his tree.
The next day, three kids came to the bench. Mr. Ike's eyes twinkled.
"Pick a card, any card," said Mr. Ike. Then he pulled it out from behind Leo's ear!
He showed them how the trick worked. Leo dropped the cards everywhere, and everyone laughed.
Soon more kids came, then a lady with a dog, then the man from the corner shop.
Every afternoon, the bench under the chestnut tree was the busiest spot on Maple Street.
Then one day, the bench was empty. The next day, it was empty again.
Mrs. Patel from upstairs told them Mr. Ike was ill in bed. "He has to rest for a whole week."
Zuri looked down at the empty bench from her window. Then she had an idea.
She called Leo and Amira. All week long, they drew and drew and drew.
On Saturday morning, they covered the whole bench in drawings and hung more from the tree.
When Mr. Ike came outside at last, he stopped and stared. Then he put his hand on his heart.
"I thought I was all alone on this street," he said softly. "But look at all my friends."
From then on, nobody on Maple Street sat alone. And it all began with one little drawing.

pageTexts: High on a hill above the village of Lowbrook lived a giant named Gertrude.
Gertrude loved her apple trees. She watered them, sang to them and let the bluebirds nest in her hair.
Her orchard grew so well that every branch bent low with apples.
Soon there were apples on the roof, apples in the chimney and apples piled up to her knees.
There were far too many to eat. Some went brown and squishy, and Gertrude hated to waste them.
Down in Lowbrook, the harvest had been poor. The pantries were nearly empty.
The villagers looked up at the hill and shivered. "Never go near the giant," they whispered.
Every evening, Gertrude looked down at the village lights. She wished that someone would visit.
A boy named Finch was hungry, and so was his little sister, Wren. "I'll go and ask the giant," said Finch.
Finch climbed the steep, rocky path. His knees were wobbly, but he kept on going.
At the top, he came to a boot as big as a boat. He looked up, and up, and up.
"H-hello," said Finch. "Please may I have one apple?" Gertrude bent down and smiled.
"Just one?" laughed Gertrude. "Take a whole cartful!" She filled a wooden cart right to the top.
Finch rolled the cart down the hill, and Gertrude held the back so it wouldn't go too fast.
The whole village came running. "Where did you get all these apples?" they gasped.
"From Gertrude," said Finch. "She isn't scary at all. She's kind, and she has more than she can eat."
The next morning, the villagers climbed the hill with baskets, buckets and wheelbarrows.
Gertrude lifted the children high so they could reach the apples at the very top.
Back in Lowbrook, the ovens were warm again. Everyone baked apple pies and apple bread.
They pressed sweet apple juice and filled jugs and jars for the long winter.
Then the villagers made Gertrude something special: an invitation as big as a door.
At the harvest feast, Gertrude sat at the end of the longest table, with lanterns glowing all around her.
They gave her the biggest apple pie ever baked in Lowbrook. Gertrude wiped away a happy tear.
Gertrude still had too many apples. But now she had something much better: friends.
